title: Act 2: The Slave Who Became King

beats.text: The man's name was *Qutb al-Din Aibak*, and he had been *a slave*.
Now, that needs explaining, because slave in this system doesn't mean what you're picturing.
Central Asian rulers deliberately bought boys, raised them,
trained them as *elite soldiers* and *administrators*, and promoted them on merit.
The whole point was that a slave had no powerful family behind him,
so he owed everything to you. It was an *insurance policy*.
The insurance policy *took over*.
In *1206*, when Ghori was assassinated, Aibak simply declared himself *Sultan of Delhi*.
A man who had been sold for money now ran northern India.
To make sure nobody forgot it, he started building a *victory tower* in Delhi.
It's called the *Qutb Minar*, it's *73 metres* of red sandstone,
it's still standing today, and it is still the *tallest stone tower in India*.
beats.fix: Script said 'tallest brick minaret on Earth' right after calling it sandstone. Britannica: tallest stone tower in India.

beats.text: He didn't live to see it finished. In *1210*, he died *playing polo*.
He fell off his horse and the saddle went through him.
One of the most powerful men in Asia, taken out by *a sport*.
What he left behind is called the *Delhi Sultanate*,
and it would run northern India for *over 300 years*.
And here's a detail I genuinely did not expect to find.
In *1236*, the throne went to *a woman*.
Her name was *Razia*.
Her father, the sultan, had four sons and looked at all of them
and concluded, out loud, that his daughter was *better than the lot*.
So he named her his heir. *The nobles hated it*.
Razia ignored them, dropped the veil, wore a tunic,
rode at the front of her own army, and ran the Sultanate for *about four years*.
Four years, and then the nobles who had never accepted her finally got her.
She was overthrown and killed in *1240*.
It would be almost *seven hundred years* before another woman ran anything in India at that level.
The Sultanate survived her. But it was about to face
the single most frightening thing in the medieval world,
arriving from the northwest with *a hundred thousand horses*.

title: Act 3: The Sultan Who Beat the Mongols and Then Fixed the Price of Onions

beats.text: The Mongols were coming. They had already flattened *Baghdad*, *Persia*, and most of *China*.
When they turned toward India, everyone assumed Delhi was finished.
The man sitting on the throne was *Alauddin Khalji*,
and he was ruthless in a very specific, very effective way.
He took the throne by inviting his own uncle, who was also the sultan,
to a friendly riverside meeting and having him beheaded there.
Family occasions in this dynasty were *tense*.
But the Mongols found him *extremely annoying*.
Between roughly *1297* and *1308*, they invaded again and again.
Once they got all the way to Delhi itself and camped outside the walls.
Alauddin beat them back *every single time*.
He built forts along the invasion routes,
kept a *permanent standing army* instead of calling up soldiers at harvest time,
and India became one of the very few places the Mongols tried repeatedly and *never took*.
But to keep a permanent army, you have to pay a permanent army.
And soldiers need to eat. And Alauddin could not afford both.
So he invented something the world had basically never seen at this scale.
He *fixed the price of everything*.
Not suggested. *Fixed*.
Grain, cloth, horses, cattle, sugar, vegetables, slaves,
everything got an *official price* set by the state.
Then he built an entire inspection bureaucracy to enforce it,
with government-run markets and *undercover agents* sent to buy things and check nobody was overcharging.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Right. Wheat is now this price.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: And if the harvest is bad?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Still that price.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: And if the harvest is amazing?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Still that price.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Sir, that's not really how markets—

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: I know exactly how markets work. That's the problem.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: What if a merchant cheats?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Then I take from him exactly what he overcharged.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Money?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Flesh. Same weight.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: ...I'll go and tell the merchants.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Tell them warmly.
It worked. Prices in Delhi stayed *flat* for years,
and his army got paid on a small salary because that salary actually bought things.
It is one of the most aggressive economic experiments of the entire medieval world
and it happened in Delhi in the year *1300*.
Alauddin died in *1316*, and within a couple of decades the throne went to a man
who was, by every account, *brilliant*. Genuinely learned.
Spoke multiple languages, studied mathematics, philosophy, medicine.
He was also about to have *two ideas* so catastrophically bad
they're still taught in Indian schools *as a warning*.

title: Act 4: The Genius Who Broke His Own Empire Twice

beats.text: His name was *Muhammad bin Tughlaq*,
and idea number one was that *Delhi was in the wrong place*.
He had a point, honestly. The empire had expanded south,
and Delhi was stuck up in the far north, weeks of travel from half his territory.
A capital in the middle would be easier to run. *Reasonable*.
His solution was to move the capital roughly *1,100 kilometres* south
to a city he renamed *Daulatabad*.
And when he said move the capital, he did not mean move the government.
He meant *move the city*.
The nobles, the clerks, the poets, the shopkeepers, ordinary families.
Everybody. Across the country. *In the heat*.
Enormous numbers of people died on the road.
And when the survivors arrived and settled in, he looked at the situation,
realised Daulatabad was too far from the northern frontier to defend against invasions,
and ordered everyone to *march back to Delhi*.
Both directions. On foot. *For nothing*.
Idea number two was *money*.
Silver was running short worldwide, so he decided to issue *token currency*:
brass and copper coins that were officially worth the same as silver ones.
Which is actually how modern money works, so in principle, *ahead of his time*.
In practice, he forgot one small thing.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: The new coins are a huge success, Your Majesty. Circulation is enormous.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Wonderful. The treasury must be full.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Full of coins, yes.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Excellent.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Not ones we made.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Sorry?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Every household with a furnace is making them, sir.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: My neighbour made forty this morning. He's a baker.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Can they do that?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: It's brass, sir. It's a pan.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: ...And they're paying their taxes with these?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Enthusiastically.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: How enthusiastically?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: We've been paid four times this year by a man who owns one goat.
He had to cancel the whole scheme and buy the fake coins back with real silver,
which emptied the treasury he was trying to fill.
The historian *Ibn Battuta*, a Moroccan traveller who actually worked as a judge in Tughlaq's court,
wrote all of it down, and his account is one of the great eyewitness documents of the medieval world.
Quick pause. If you're enjoying this, a like genuinely helps more than a wheelbarrow of brass coins.
And unlike the coins, *it's free*.
And stay with me, because everything so far has been invaders taking gold and going home.
In about fifteen minutes, a trading company in London with shareholders and a quarterly dividend
is going to walk in, buy this entire country with a bribe,
and then do something no invader in a thousand years had managed.
The Sultanate never recovered. Provinces broke away one after another.
And down in the south, in the middle of that chaos, two brothers founded a city
that would become, for a while, the richest place any European had ever laid eyes on.
